title: Sticky Habits
tagline: Systems that work when motivation disappears.
description: A 60-card playbook for building habits that actually last.

modules.title: The Motivation Myth
modules.summary: Why feelings are a terrible foundation.

cards.content: Motivation is a feeling that rises and falls with your mood, energy, and circumstances. It was never meant to be your daily engine.
Relying on motivation is like steering your life by the wind instead of the rudder. You end up wherever the breeze takes you.
The days you need habits most are usually the days motivation ghosts you. That's exactly when systems matter.
Successful people don't feel more motivated than you. They just built habits that don't need constant emotional fuel.
Habits run on autopilot. Motivation requires conscious effort every single time. One scales. The other burns out.
Think of motivation as the spark that starts the fire. Habits are the wood that keeps it burning long after the match is gone.
The biggest lie in self-improvement is that you need to feel ready before you begin. Action creates the feeling, not the other way around.
When motivation fades, identity takes over. The question shifts from 'Do I feel like it?' to 'Who am I becoming?'
Discipline isn't about forcing yourself harder. It's about designing a life where the right actions become the default path.
Drop the motivation chase. Build small systems instead. They carry you through the flat, boring, and tough days.

modules.title: The Habit Loop
modules.summary: The simple mechanics behind automatic behavior.

cards.content: Every habit follows the same loop: cue, craving, response, reward. Master these four parts and you control the behavior.
The cue is the trigger that tells your brain it's time to act. It can be a time, place, emotion, or previous action.
Craving is the motivational force. It's the desire for the reward that powers the habit.
The response is the actual habit you perform. It can be a thought or an action depending on how complex it is.
The reward satisfies the craving and teaches your brain that this loop is worth remembering for next time.
To build a new habit, make the cue obvious, the craving attractive, the response easy, and the reward satisfying.
To break a bad habit, do the opposite: hide the cue, make it unattractive, difficult, and unsatisfying.
Your current habits were built by this loop running on repeat, often without you noticing.
Once a habit becomes automatic, the cue and reward become linked directly in your brain.
Understanding the loop gives you the operating manual for your own behavior.
The secret to building habits that stick is to start so small that you can't say no. Scale beats intensity.
Two push-ups a day beats fifty push-ups once a month. Consistency compounds faster than perfection.
Tiny habits lower the activation energy so dramatically that your brain stops negotiating with you.
Flossing one tooth, drinking one glass of water, or writing one sentence builds the identity of someone who follows through.
Once the tiny version is automatic, you naturally expand it without forcing motivation.
Small starts protect you from the all-or-nothing trap that kills most habit attempts.
Your brain loves quick wins. Tiny habits give it dopamine hits that reinforce the behavior early.
Scale up only after the habit has survived at least two weeks of daily tiny reps.
The gold is not in doing more on good days. It's in never missing on the days you don't feel like it.
Start stupid small. The compound effect will shock you months later.

modules.title: Stack and Design
modules.summary: Habit stacking and environment hacks that make it effortless.

cards.content: Habit stacking attaches a new behavior to an existing habit using the formula: After I [current habit], I will [new habit].
Your environment is the invisible hand shaping your habits. Design it so good choices are obvious and easy.
Want to read more? Put the book on your pillow instead of hiding it in a drawer.
Reduce friction for good habits. Increase friction for bad ones. This beats willpower every time.
Prime your environment for success the night before. Set out workout clothes, prep healthy snacks, or block distracting apps.
Context is the cue. Change your surroundings and you change the habits that show up automatically.
Make good habits attractive by pairing them with something you already enjoy, like listening to a podcast only while walking.
One small change in your space can trigger a cascade of better behaviors without extra effort.
The people around you are part of your environment. Surround yourself with those who embody the habits you want.
Design your defaults so that the path of least resistance leads straight to your goals.

modules.title: When It Gets Hard
modules.summary: Handling resistance, plateaus, and ghosted motivation.

cards.content: The first weeks feel fresh. Then boredom and resistance show up. This is where most habits die.
Never miss twice. One missed day is a mistake. Two in a row starts a new pattern.
When motivation is gone, fall back on your minimum viable habit. Do the tiny version no matter what.
Plateaus happen when the novelty wears off. That's your signal to add a new layer or tweak the stack.
Track your streak but focus on identity. Ask: What would the person I want to become do today?
Use the two-day rule for flexibility. You can miss one day, but never two consecutive days.
Resistance is information. It often points to where your habit needs better design, not more willpower.
On bad days, show up anyway. Even a 10% effort keeps the chain alive and your identity intact.
Recommit to your why, but anchor it in identity rather than fleeting outcomes.
The difference between people who succeed and those who don't is what they do on the days they don't feel like it.

modules.title: Make It Last
modules.summary: Systems for identity, tracking, and long-term consistency.

cards.content: Habits stick best when they become part of who you are. Shift from 'I want to run' to 'I am a runner.'
Track your habits simply. A calendar chain or simple yes/no log creates powerful visual proof of progress.
Celebrate small wins immediately. A quick internal 'nice' or fist pump reinforces the loop.
Review your habits monthly. Drop what no longer serves you and double down on what does.
Build recovery systems. Know exactly how you'll restart after travel, illness, or life chaos.
Identity change is the strongest force. Every action is a vote for the person you want to become.
Habits compound. The daily 1% improvements feel invisible until suddenly they're not.
Share your habits with others or join a group. Social accountability turns individual effort into community norm.
Make it satisfying long-term by focusing on the process and the person you're becoming, not just distant results.
The ultimate habit is becoming someone who doesn't quit on themselves. Systems make that identity real.
